kangaroo-at-2021-junior-01.title: Check the step from year to year
kangaroo-at-2021-junior-01.body:
A date moves back by one weekday each year, and by two after a 29 February. From 17/3/2022 the third Thursday moves to 16/3/2023 (one day earlier, correct). 2024 is a leap year, so 16 March 2024 is a Saturday, and the Thursdays of March 2024 are 7, 14, 21, 28. The third Thursday is the 21st, not the 14th. (From 21/3/2024 the next ones are 20/3/2025 and 19/3/2026, as listed.)

**Answer: (C) 14/3/2024**

kangaroo-at-2021-junior-01.title: Third Thursday is between the 15th and the 21st
kangaroo-at-2021-junior-01.body:
The third Thursday of any month is always one of the days 15 to 21 (the first Thursday is one of days 1 to 7). The date 14/3/2024 is too early, so it must be the wrong one.

**Answer: (C) 14/3/2024**

kangaroo-at-2021-junior-02.title: Follow the ups and downs
kangaroo-at-2021-junior-02.body:
The temperatures are $-1, -2, 0, 6, 2$. So the graph goes slightly down (Fri to Sat), then up a little (to $0$), then up a lot (to $6$), and finally down (to $2$). Only graph (B) has the pattern: small drop, small rise, big rise, drop.

**Answer: (B)**

kangaroo-at-2021-junior-03.title: Split into slanted and horizontal parts
kangaroo-at-2021-junior-03.body:
Let the side be $s$. In each path, the slanted pieces together cover every height level exactly once (some on the left side, some on the right), so they add up to one full side $s$. Every path also uses the whole bottom side $s$. The difference lies in the horizontal segments inside the triangle: a horizontal segment at a lower level is longer.

Call the three dotted levels, from top to bottom, 1, 2, 3, with widths $w_1 < w_2 < w_3$. From the figure, $P$ uses levels 1 and 2, $Q$ uses levels 2 and 3, and $R$ uses levels 1 and 3. So
$$P = 2s + w_1 + w_2,\quad R = 2s + w_1 + w_3,\quad Q = 2s + w_2 + w_3,$$
which gives $P < R < Q$.

**Answer: (B) $P<R<Q$**

kangaroo-at-2021-junior-04.title: Go from rectangle to rectangle
kangaroo-at-2021-junior-04.body:
The rectangle with area 18 has height 6, so the left column has width $18 : 6 = 3$. The rectangle with area 12 in the same column then has height $12 : 3 = 4$. The rectangle with area 16 lies in the same row as the 12 (same height 4), so the middle column has width $16 : 4 = 4$. The rectangle with area 32 in that column then has height $32 : 4 = 8$. The rectangle with area 48 is in the same row as the 32 (height 8), so the right column has width $48 : 8 = 6$. Finally, the bottom right rectangle has height $30 : 6 = 5$ cm.

**Answer: (B) 5 cm**

kangaroo-at-2021-junior-05.title: Set up an equation
kangaroo-at-2021-junior-05.body:
Let the visitors score $k$ goals in the second half; the home team scores $2k$. Final score: $(9 + 2k) : (14 + k)$. The home team wins by one: $9 + 2k = 15 + k$, so $k = 6$, and the score is $21:20$.

**Answer: (B) 21:20**

kangaroo-at-2021-junior-05.title: Count the gap
kangaroo-at-2021-junior-05.body:
The home team starts 5 goals behind and must end 1 goal ahead, so it must gain 6 goals in the second half. Scoring twice as many as the opponents, it gains exactly as many goals as the opponents score, so the visitors score 6 and the home team 12. Final score $21:20$.

**Answer: (B) 21:20**

kangaroo-at-2021-junior-06.title: Total of the ages
kangaroo-at-2021-junior-06.body:
The band has 6 members with average 21, so the ages add up to $6 \cdot 21 = 126$. The other three members add up to $19 + 20 + 21 = 60$, so the three friends add up to $66$, and each is $66 : 3 = 22$ years old.

**Answer: (C) 22**

kangaroo-at-2021-junior-06.title: Deviations from the average
kangaroo-at-2021-junior-06.body:
Compared with 21, the members aged 19, 20, 21 are $-2, -1, 0$ in total $-3$. The three equal ages must make up $+3$, i.e. each is $1$ above the average: $22$.

**Answer: (C) 22**

kangaroo-at-2021-junior-07.title: Cut into small triangles
kangaroo-at-2021-junior-07.body:
The six rhombuses meet at the centre, so each has an angle of $360^\circ : 6 = 60^\circ$ there; each rhombus consists of two equilateral triangles of area $2.5$ cm$^2$. Between two neighbouring rhombuses there is a gap triangle formed by two sides of length $s$ (the side of the rhombus) enclosing the angle $360^\circ - 120^\circ - 120^\circ = 120^\circ$; its area is $\tfrac12 s^2 \sin 120^\circ = \tfrac{\sqrt3}{4}s^2$, the same as one equilateral triangle, i.e. $2.5$ cm$^2$. The hexagon consists of the 6 rhombuses and the 6 gaps: $6 \cdot 5 + 6 \cdot 2.5 = 45$ cm$^2$.

**Answer: (C) 45 cm$^2$**

kangaroo-at-2021-junior-07.title: Count equilateral triangles
kangaroo-at-2021-junior-07.body:
The hexagon can be tiled by equilateral triangles of side $s$ (each rhombus gives 2) and by the 6 gap triangles, each equivalent in area to one such triangle. That is $12 + 6 = 18$ units of $2.5$ cm$^2$, i.e. $45$ cm$^2$.

**Answer: (C) 45 cm$^2$**

kangaroo-at-2021-junior-08.title: Subtract the square's side
kangaroo-at-2021-junior-08.body:
The square has side 3 cm. Let the big rectangle have width $W$ and height $H$, so $W + H = 15$. Rectangle $ABCD$ (opposite the square) has sides $W - 3$ and $H - 3$, so its perimeter is $2(W - 3 + H - 3) = 2(15 - 6) = 18$ cm.

**Answer: (C) 18 cm**

kangaroo-at-2021-junior-08.title: Example
kangaroo-at-2021-junior-08.body:
Take, for example, a $10 \times 5$ rectangle (perimeter 30). Then $ABCD$ is $7 \times 2$, with perimeter 18 cm. Since the answer does not depend on the shape (first solution), it is always 18 cm.

**Answer: (C) 18 cm**

kangaroo-at-2021-junior-09.title: Use the three conditions
kangaroo-at-2021-junior-09.body:
The first triangle shown is right-angled with legs 4 and 5 (area 10, not isosceles). The second is right-angled and isosceles with legs 4 and 4 (area 8). Already two triangles are right-angled, so the third must not be right-angled. Only one is isosceles, so the third must be isosceles. And its area must be 8 or 10.

Triangle (D) has a horizontal base of 4 and its apex 4 units below the middle of the base: it is isosceles, not right-angled (its base angles are $\arctan 2 \approx 63^\circ$), and its area is $\tfrac12 \cdot 4 \cdot 4 = 8$. It fits all conditions. The others fail: (B) and (E) are right-angled, (C) is isosceles but has area 12, and (A) is neither isosceles nor of area 8 or 10.

**Answer: (D)**

kangaroo-at-2021-junior-10.title: Check the options
kangaroo-at-2021-junior-10.body:
For $x = \frac19$: $\frac19 - \frac1{10} = \frac{1}{90}$ and $\frac19 \cdot \frac1{10} = \frac1{90}$, equal. For example $x = \frac1{10}$ gives $0$ and $\frac1{100}$, not equal.

**Answer: (E) $\frac{1}{9}$**

kangaroo-at-2021-junior-11.title: Time between lightings
kangaroo-at-2021-junior-11.body:
Nine-tenths of a sparkler burn in $0.9 \cdot 2 = 1.8$ min. The second sparkler is lit $1.8$ min after the first, the third $1.8$ min after the second, and so on: the tenth is lit after $9 \cdot 1.8 = 16.2$ min and burns for another $2$ min. Total $18.2$ min $= 18$ min $12$ s.

**Answer: (B) 18 min 12 sec**

kangaroo-at-2021-junior-11.title: Count burnt lengths
kangaroo-at-2021-junior-11.body:
While a sparkler's last tenth burns, the next one is burning too, so that tenth adds no extra time. The time is therefore that of $9 \cdot \tfrac{9}{10} + 1 = 9.1$ sparkler lengths burning one after another: $9.1 \cdot 2 = 18.2$ min $= 18$ min $12$ s.

**Answer: (B) 18 min 12 sec**

kangaroo-at-2021-junior-12.title: Fibonacci up to step 5
kangaroo-at-2021-junior-12.body:
The number of ways to reach step $n$ is the sum of the ways to reach steps $n-1$ and $n-2$. Steps 1 to 5: $1, 2, 3, 5, 8$. Step 6 cannot be used. To get past it he must go from step 5 to step 7 (a 2-step), and then from 7 to 8 (a 1-step; 6 to 8 is impossible). So there are $8$ ways.

**Answer: (C) 8**

kangaroo-at-2021-junior-12.title: Fixed part of the route
kangaroo-at-2021-junior-12.body:
Since step 6 is forbidden, every route passes through step 5, then jumps to 7, then steps to 8. The only freedom is how to reach step 5 with 1- and 2-steps: with zero 2-steps (1 way), one 2-step (4 ways: $\binom41$), or two 2-steps (3 ways: $\binom32$). Total $1 + 4 + 3 = 8$.

**Answer: (C) 8**

kangaroo-at-2021-junior-13.title: Use the pairs of rings
kangaroo-at-2021-junior-13.body:
Each pair of rings meets in 2 of the circles, and each ring passes through 4 circles (its intersections with the two other rings). Let $x$, $y$, $z$ be the sums of the two numbers shared by the top and left ring, the top and right ring, and the left and right ring. Each number lies on exactly two rings, so the three ring sums add up to $2(1+2+\dots+6) = 42$; each ring sum is $14$. The top ring gives $x + y = 14$, the left ring $x + z = 14$, the right ring $y + z = 14$, so $x = y = z = 7$.

The question mark and the 6 are the two intersections of the left and right rings, so $? = 7 - 6 = 1$.

**Answer: (A) 1**

kangaroo-at-2021-junior-14.title: Use the least common multiple
kangaroo-at-2021-junior-14.body:
A number $n$ has remainder 5 when divided by 6, 7, 8 and 9 exactly when $n - 5$ is divisible by all four, i.e. by $\operatorname{lcm}(6,7,8,9) = 504$. So $n = 5 + 504k$: $5, 509, 1013, 1517, 2021, \dots$ The ones below 2021 are $5, 509, 1013, 1517$: four numbers.

**Answer: (A) 4**

kangaroo-at-2021-junior-14.title: Count down from 2021
kangaroo-at-2021-junior-14.body:
$2021 - 5 = 2016 = 4 \cdot 504$, so the numbers with the property below 2021 are $2021 - 504k$ for $k = 1, 2, 3, 4$, i.e. $1517, 1013, 509, 5$. That makes 4.

**Answer: (A) 4**

kangaroo-at-2021-junior-15.title: Isosceles triangles with radii
kangaroo-at-2021-junior-15.body:
Let $M$ and $N$ be the left and right ends of the diameter, $X$ the point on the arc with the $32^\circ$ angle and $Y$ the point on the arc with the marked (dotted) angle. The dotted angle $MYN$ is $90^\circ$, since it is inscribed in a semicircle.

$OY = ON$, so triangle $OYN$ is isosceles and $\angle OYN = \angle ONY = 67^\circ$. Hence $\angle MYO = 90^\circ - 67^\circ = 23^\circ$.

$OX = OY$, so triangle $OXY$ is isosceles and $\angle OYX = \angle OXY = 32^\circ$.

The angle $\alpha$ lies between $YX$ and $YM$: $\alpha = \angle OYX - \angle MYO = 32^\circ - 23^\circ = 9^\circ$.

**Answer: (A) $9^\circ$**

kangaroo-at-2021-junior-16.title: Divisibility by 4
kangaroo-at-2021-junior-16.body:
The teams total $9 + 15 + 17 + 19 + 21 = 81$ people. After one team starts, the rest are boys $b$ and girls $3b$, so the remaining number $4b$ is divisible by 4. $81 - t$ is divisible by 4 for $t = 9, 17, 21$ (giving 72, 64, 60).

- $t = 9$: $b = 18$, but no group of the teams 15, 17, 19, 21 adds up to 18.
- $t = 17$: $b = 16$, impossible with teams 9, 15, 19, 21.
- $t = 21$: $b = 15$, the team of 15 are boys, and the girls are $9 + 17 + 19 = 45 = 3 \cdot 15$. ✓

So the team of 21 has started.

**Answer: (E) 21**

kangaroo-at-2021-junior-17.title: Count the pairs that changed order
kangaroo-at-2021-junior-17.body:
Every pair of cars whose order at the finish differs from the order at the start needs at least one overtaking, and with exactly one overtaking per such pair the final order can be reached. The start order (reading the rows the same way) is I, II, III, IV, V and the finish order is III, V, I, IV, II.

Pairs that swapped: III with I and II (2 pairs); V with I, IV, II (3 pairs); IV with II (1 pair). Pairs I–IV, III–IV, III–V, I–II keep their order. In total $2 + 3 + 1 = 6$ pairs swapped, so at least 6 points were awarded, and 6 is achievable.

**Answer: (E) 6**

kangaroo-at-2021-junior-17.title: Build the finish order
kangaroo-at-2021-junior-17.body:
Starting from I, II, III, IV, V, move the cars one adjacent swap at a time (each swap is one overtaking): III passes II and I (2 swaps): III, I, II, IV, V. V passes IV, II, I (3 swaps): III, V, I, II, IV. IV passes II (1 swap): III, V, I, IV, II. That is 6 overtakings, and fewer is impossible because each of these 6 pairs had to change order.

**Answer: (E) 6**

kangaroo-at-2021-junior-18.title: Count how often each sub-square is used
kangaroo-at-2021-junior-18.body:
There are four $2\times2$ sub-squares: top-left, top-right, bottom-left, bottom-right, used $a$, $b$, $c$, $d$ times. Every sub-square contains the centre, so the centre is $a + b + c + d = 47$. The top middle cell lies in the top-left and top-right sub-squares: $a + b = 18$. The bottom-left corner lies only in the bottom-left sub-square: $c = 13$. The bottom-right corner lies only in the bottom-right sub-square, so $? = d = 47 - 18 - 13 = 16$.

**Answer: (C) 16**

kangaroo-at-2021-junior-19.title: Use the interior angle sum
kangaroo-at-2021-junior-19.body:
The mountain together with the bottom edge is a hexagon whose interior angles add up to $(6 - 2)\cdot 180^\circ = 720^\circ$. The marked angles are the parts of the circles outside the mountain. At the four upper vertices (two peaks, the valley and the bend on the right slope) the marked angle is $360^\circ$ minus the interior angle. At the two vertices on the bottom edge, the marked angle is the part above the bottom line outside the mountain, i.e. $180^\circ$ minus the interior angle. So the sum is
$$4 \cdot 360^\circ + 2 \cdot 180^\circ - 720^\circ = 1080^\circ.$$

**Answer: (C) $1080^\circ$**

kangaroo-at-2021-junior-21.title: Law of sines
kangaroo-at-2021-junior-21.body:
In triangle $ABC$ the angles at $A$ and $C$ are $75^\circ$ and $60^\circ$, so $\angle B = 45^\circ$. The stairs consist of horizontal and vertical pieces; their total length is the horizontal plus the vertical distance from $A$ to $B$. Since $AB$ makes $45^\circ$ with the horizontal line $BC$, both distances equal $\frac{AB}{\sqrt2}$, so the stairs have length $\sqrt2 \cdot AB$.

By the law of sines, $\frac{AC}{\sin 45^\circ} = \frac{AB}{\sin 60^\circ}$, so $AC = AB \cdot \frac{\sqrt2/2}{\sqrt3/2} = AB\cdot\frac{\sqrt2}{\sqrt3}$. The ratio is
$$\frac{AC}{\sqrt2\, AB} = \frac{1}{\sqrt3} = \frac{\sqrt3}{3}.$$

**Answer: (E) $\frac{\sqrt3}{3}$**

kangaroo-at-2021-junior-21.title: Use the height
kangaroo-at-2021-junior-21.body:
Let $H$ be the foot of the altitude from $A$ and $h = AH$. Since $\angle B = 45^\circ$, $BH = h$ and the stairs have length $BH + AH = 2h$. Since $\angle C = 60^\circ$, $AC = \frac{h}{\sin 60^\circ} = \frac{2h}{\sqrt3}$. The ratio is $\frac{2h/\sqrt3}{2h} = \frac{1}{\sqrt3} = \frac{\sqrt3}{3}$.

**Answer: (E) $\frac{\sqrt3}{3}$**

kangaroo-at-2021-junior-23.title: Find N
kangaroo-at-2021-junior-23.body:
To make $N$ as small as possible, it should have as few digits as possible, so as many 9s as possible: $2021 = 224 \cdot 9 + 5$. So $N$ has 225 digits, and the smallest such number puts the small digit in front: $N = 5\underbrace{99\ldots9}_{224}$, i.e. $N = 6 \cdot 10^{224} - 1$.

Then $N + 2021 = 6 \cdot 10^{224} + 2020$, whose digits are a 6, zeros, and then $2, 0, 2, 0$. The digit sum is $6 + 2 + 2 = 10$.

**Answer: (A) 10**

kangaroo-at-2021-junior-23.title: Add by hand
kangaroo-at-2021-junior-23.body:
Adding $2021$ to $5 99\ldots 999$: the last four digits $9999 + 2021 = 12020$, so we write $2020$ and carry 1. The carry turns all the remaining 9s into 0s and finally the leading 5 into 6. The result is $600\ldots02020$ with digit sum $6 + 2 + 2 = 10$.

**Answer: (A) 10**

kangaroo-at-2021-junior-24.title: Count shared words
kangaroo-at-2021-junior-24.body:
Call the third boy Xavi. Let $t$ be the number of words all three wrote, and $p_{SJ}$, $p_{SX}$, $p_{JX}$ the numbers of words written by exactly two of them. A boy loses 2 points (compared with 30) for every word he shares with exactly one other boy and 3 points for each word shared by all three. So
$$S = 30 - 2p_{SJ} - 2p_{SX} - 3t,\quad J = 30 - 2p_{SJ} - 2p_{JX} - 3t,\quad X = 30 - 2p_{SX} - 2p_{JX} - 3t.$$
$S = 19$ gives $2(p_{SJ} + p_{SX}) + 3t = 11$, so $t$ is odd: $t = 1$ with $p_{SJ} + p_{SX} = 4$, or $t = 3$ with $p_{SJ} + p_{SX} = 1$.

$J > X$ means $p_{SX} > p_{SJ}$, and $X > S$ means $p_{SJ} > p_{JX} \ge 0$, so $p_{SJ} \ge 1$ and $p_{SX} \ge 2$. This rules out $t = 3$ and leaves $p_{SJ} = 1$, $p_{SX} = 3$, $p_{JX} = 0$, $t = 1$. Then $J = 30 - 2 - 0 - 3 = 25$.

**Answer: (E) 25**

kangaroo-at-2021-junior-25.title: Coordinates
kangaroo-at-2021-junior-25.body:
Put the common lower vertex at the origin, so the smaller square is $[0,4]\times[0,4]$. The next vertex of the larger square lies on the right side of the smaller square, at $(4, h)$. The sides of the larger square are the vectors $(4, h)$ and $(-h, 4)$, so its left vertex is $(-h, 4)$ (at the height of the top side of the small square, as in the picture) and its top vertex is $(4 - h, 4 + h)$.

The grey triangle has vertices $(-h, 4)$, $(0, 4)$ and $(4-h, 4+h)$: its base along the line $y = 4$ has length $h$ and its height is $h$. So $\tfrac12 h^2 = 1$, $h^2 = 2$. The larger square has area $4^2 + h^2 = 18$.

**Answer: (B) 18**

kangaroo-at-2021-junior-26.title: Factor the difference

kangaroo-at-2021-junior-27.title: Remove the empty row and column
kangaroo-at-2021-junior-27.body:
The rows need $2, 0, 2, 1$ black cells and the columns $2, 0, 2, 1$. The second row and the second column stay white, so we have to paint a $3 \times 3$ table (rows 1, 3, 4 and columns 1, 3, 4) with row counts $2, 2, 1$ and column counts $2, 2, 1$.

The last row has one black cell.

- If it is in the last column, rows 1 and 3 must both be black in columns 1 and 3: 1 way.
- If it is in column 1, column 1 needs one more black cell and column 3 two; rows 1 and 3 are both black in column 3, and each needs one more cell, one in column 1 and one in column 4: 2 ways.
- If it is in column 3, by symmetry: 2 ways.

In total $1 + 2 + 2 = 5$ ways.

**Answer: (D) 5**

kangaroo-at-2021-junior-28.title: Split into factors
kangaroo-at-2021-junior-28.body:
$1000 = 2^3 \cdot 5^3$. A digit divisible by 5 must be 5 itself, so exactly three of the digits are 5. The other two digits multiply to 8: they are $\{1, 8\}$ or $\{2, 4\}$. For the digits $5,5,5,1,8$ there are $\frac{5!}{3!} = 20$ arrangements, and for $5,5,5,2,4$ also 20. In total 40 numbers.

**Answer: (D) 40**

kangaroo-at-2021-junior-29.title: Build the weights from the smallest
kangaroo-at-2021-junior-29.body:
Order the weights $w_1 < w_2 < \dots < w_8$. The hardest test for a set of four coins $a < b < c < d$ is $d$ together with $a$ against $b$ and $c$, so we need $a + d > b + c$ for all such choices. For a fixed heaviest coin $w_k$ the worst case is $a = w_1$, $b = w_{k-2}$, $c = w_{k-1}$, so the condition is
$$w_k > w_{k-1} + w_{k-2} - w_1 \quad (k = 4, \dots, 8).$$
To keep everything small take $w_1 = 1$, $w_2 = 2$, $w_3 = 3$; then $w_k \ge w_{k-1} + w_{k-2}$:
$$1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13, 21, 34.$$
This set works, and the same inequalities show that for any valid set $w_k - w_1 \ge (w_{k-1} - w_1) + (w_{k-2} - w_1) + 1$, which forces $w_8 - w_1 \ge 33$, i.e. $w_8 \ge 34$. So the answer is 34 g.

**Answer: (C) 34 g**

kangaroo-at-2021-junior-30.title: The colouring repeats every 5
kangaroo-at-2021-junior-30.body:
Each block of five consecutive balls has one red, one yellow, one blue and two green balls. Comparing the blocks $k, \dots, k+4$ and $k+1, \dots, k+5$, ball $k+5$ has the same colour as ball $k$. So the colour depends only on the remainder of the number mod 5.

Balls 2, 20, 202 are green, i.e. remainders 2 and 0 are green (and these are the two green remainders). The remainders 1, 3, 4 get red, yellow, blue. A red ball is followed by a yellow one: red at remainder 1 would need yellow at 2 (green), red at 4 would need yellow at 0 (green), so red is at 3 and yellow at 4. Blue is at remainder 1. Since $2021 \equiv 1 \pmod 5$, ball 2021 is blue.

**Answer: (D) blue**
